summary.summary: Brent's 2024/25 outturn shows external borrowing up £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m, funding a capital programme that pushed the Loan CFR up £102.6m to £1,357.1m (General Fund £1,015.1m, HRA £342.0m). A £13.7m budget variance on capital financing costs (£41.5m actual against a £27.8m budget) was offset by a drawdown from capital reserves. The council has grown related-party lending to its wholly-owned housing companies — £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing — and holds £59.5m of LOBO loans, of which £35.0m face an interest-rate review in 2025/26.

signals.headline: External borrowing rose £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m in 2024/25, from £170.0m of new loans against £84.2m of repayments.
signals.why: A rapid, double-digit rise in the debt stock within a single year.

signals.headline: A £13.7m capital-financing budget variance (£41.5m actual vs £27.8m budget) was offset by drawing down capital reserves.
signals.why: Financing costs are already outrunning budget, absorbed by reserves rather than a revised budget.

signals.headline: £35.0m of the council's £59.5m LOBO book (5 loans) is due an interest-rate review in 2025/26.
signals.why: If a lender exercises its option the council's own option is to repay at par, which is what councils do: every LOBO call we hold — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Barnet, Brighton and Hove, Bristol — was repaid rather than accepted. So the exposure is finding £35.0m and replacing that funding at today's rates, not paying a higher rate on it.

signals.headline: Loans to Brent's wholly-owned companies stood at £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing at 31 March 2025, both secured on company property, plus a £36.4m equity stake in I4B.
signals.why: Sizeable related-party credit exposure sits alongside the headline treasury debt figures.

news_drafts.headline: Brent pension fund reports 113% funding level at 2025 valuation, up from 87% in 2022
news_drafts.lead:
Brent's pension fund is in surplus, with a funding level of 113% at its 2025 valuation, against 87% at the 2022 valuation. The figure appears in the risk register presented to the council's Pension Board on 5 November 2026.

The register reports the whole-fund valuation results, which were presented to the Pension Fund Sub-Committee in October 2025. It says: "the Brent Fund now maintains a 113% funding level and is in surplus, compared to 87% in the 2022 valuation". A funding level compares the fund's assets with the cost of the pensions it has promised to pay.

The paper also records that the fund's prudence level on the key discount rate assumption was increased to 80%. The discount rate is the rate used to turn future pension payments into a value today. The papers give no further detail on the surplus or on what it means for contributions.

news_drafts.headline: Brent forecasts £9.0m overspend on £501.8m budget at quarter 2, £0.5m better than quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Brent Council forecasts that it will overspend its general fund, the account that pays for day-to-day services other than council housing, by £9.0m in 2026/27. The quarter 2 forecast, in papers before the Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee on 20 October, is £0.5m better than at quarter 1. The revised budget is £501.8m. The papers say the overspend would require a transfer from unallocated reserves (money put aside) if it lasts to year-end.

Directorates have found £2.7m of in-year savings since quarter 1, alongside spending controls. Of £10.4m of savings agreed by full council in February 2026, £8.8m is completed or on track. The largest overspend is in Housing Needs and Support, forecast at £7.7m, which is £1.8m better than at quarter 1. The papers say rising homelessness and a shortage of suitable temporary accommodation are forecast to result in it. Households in nightly paid accommodation rose from 1,428 in April to 1,517 by the end of August. The council is pursuing more housing supply, renegotiated costs, moves to lower-cost accommodation and alternative leasing.

The housing revenue account, the separate account for the council's own homes, paid for by rents, is forecast to overspend by £3.5m. Its balanced budget is £84.4m, against forecast spending of £87.9m. One paper cites repairs and maintenance costs, new duties under Awaab's Law on damp and mould, and building-safety compliance. The other lists waking watch arrangements, council tax and service charges on new properties, and additional borrowing costs. It names the relatively low reserve position as a continuing risk.

news_drafts.headline: Brent forecasts £9.0m overspend on £501.8m budget, £0.5m better than Q1, with homelessness the largest pressure
news_drafts.lead:
Brent Council forecasts spending £9.0m more than its £501.8m day-to-day budget for 2026/27, according to the second-quarter financial report going to Cabinet on 12 October. That is £0.5m better than the first-quarter forecast. Directorates have found £2.7m of in-year savings since then, but if the overspend lasts to the year end it would be covered by a transfer from the council's unallocated reserves, money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected.

The biggest single pressure is Housing Needs and Support, forecast to overspend by £7.7m. The council was housing 1,517 households in nightly paid accommodation at the end of August, up from 1,428 in April. It received 8,795 homelessness applications in 2025/26, 21% more than the year before. Average nightly placement costs are running about £10 above budget, which the report says could add £3.9m. The £8m of growth built into the base budget does not cover these pressures.

Adult Social Care is forecasting a £1.5m overspend despite £25.7m of budget growth. Service users rose 6% in 2025/26 and 3% in 2026/27, and new care packages cost 14-16% more than those ending. Dementia-related residential placements are up 30%. Separately, the housing revenue account, the ring-fenced account for council homes paid for by rents, is forecast to overspend by £3.5m. The report cites repairs costs, new duties under Awaab's Law and building-safety work following the Regulator's C3 judgement.

findings.headline: LCIV is slowing private credit deployment, particularly into seeded funds, citing AI-driven disruption to software and business-services borrowers.
findings.detail: The paper says the risk is that rapid AI-driven disruption could lead to materially higher defaults in a tail-risk scenario, with private credit more exposed than public markets. It also says the Fidelity-type credit portfolio is outside SAA range and that detailed manager selection is underway for a new credit portfolio in the second half of the year.
findings.matters: A large institutional allocator slowing lending into a sector of borrowers is relevant to any lender, and to finance directors whose councils hold exposure to private credit.
findings.figures: 0.6% (quarter, fund); 1.5% (1 year, fund); 2.0% (1 year, index); 1.9% p.a. (3 years, relative); £80m (fund value)
findings.quote: Against this backdrop, we are slowing deployment particularly into seeded funds.

findings.headline: OTA Offshore – 2003 US Fund returned -15.2% in the quarter after OTA wrote down its holding in Park Energy, a Mexican gas pipeline operator, in November 2025.
findings.detail: The write-down in one of the fund's investments is the stated driver of the quarter's performance. The investment team is meeting the manager to understand the causes and plans to protect and recover value.
findings.matters: A single write-down causing a 15% quarterly fall in a £15m private equity holding is a specific loss event that other funds with OTA exposure would track.
findings.quote: In November 2025 OTA wrote down the value of its holding in Park Energy, a Mexican gas pipeline operator.

findings.headline: The JP Morgan Infrastructure Fund returned -5.0% over one year against a 2.5% index, a relative return of -7.5%.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall to the fund's investment in the Tata Infrastructure fund, citing sector rotation away from cyclical capex-linked stocks and high exposure to mid and small cap names. It also reports £22m called down from commitments in the quarter. The text gives £38m of outstanding commitments, while Appendix 4 shows £0m outstanding for the same fund.
findings.matters: Capital called from commitments and a fund that is both drawing down and underperforming are the kind of pension investment exposures a finance director at a council with an LGPS fund would need to track.
findings.figures: -5.0% (1 year, fund); 2.5% (1 year, index); -7.5% (1 year, relative); -2.0% (quarter, fund); £22m (called down in quarter); £38m (outstanding, per text); £0m (outstanding, Appendix 4)
findings.quote: Performance has continued to struggle this quarter with the strategy underperforming by 3.6%, and 7.5% over the one year.

findings.headline: A multi-asset credit transition scheduled for Q2 2026 should save annual fees of c. £80,000.
findings.detail: The Implementation Plan update lists a multi-asset credit transition, with £55m sold and £55m bought in MAC, as scheduled for Q2 2026. The paper says this should save the fees shown, and it is a forecast rather than a realised saving.
findings.matters: A planned fee reduction on a sizeable mandate is a concrete saving that other pension funds in the pool could compare against their own fee arrangements.
findings.quote: The multi asset credit transition is scheduled for Q2 2026. This should save annual fees of c. £80,000.

findings.headline: The Scheme returned 3.4% over the 12 months to end December 2025 against a 6.7% strategic target, while its 3-year (9.2% p.a.) and 5-year (12.6% p.a.) returns exceeded that target.
findings.detail: The paper states that the 3- and 5-year targets have been achieved but that the Scheme did not achieve its target over the last year, which it attributes to subdued returns across all asset classes. It names the Equities book and the under-performance of private markets as contributors.
findings.matters: A pension fund's return against its target feeds into the employer contribution assumptions a finance director has to plan around, and a one-year miss sits alongside multi-year outperformance.

daily_post.headline: The schedule gives end dates of 'May 1930' and 'Feb 1935' for two contracts and lists the Barnardo's Family Wellbeing Centre at £575,461.38 twice.
daily_post.lead: Duplicate entries and impossible dates in a contract register would distort any total of commitments drawn from it, which is a data-quality point finance officers would check before relying on the schedule.
